analysis.event: Post‐chikungunya joint pain (relapse) reported by Ankita Balar Arya; not a new infection, chronic joint pain after recovery.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: Approximately 25% of chikungunya patients develop chronic joint pain; 10‐15% have long‐term joint involvement >1 year; risk factors include age >45, female sex, pre‐existing joint disease; true reinfection is extremely rare.

analysis.brief_en: Post‐chikungunya joint pain, often described as a relapse, can reappear months after the acute fever has resolved. A Medindia report by Ankita Balar Arya (Aug 15 2026) notes that the pain may affect fingers, knees or ankles and can be mistaken for a new infection, though true reinfection with chikungunya is extremely rare. WHO states that long‐lasting neutralizing antibodies usually protect against future infection, while research on reinfection remains ongoing. Approximately one‐quarter of chikungunya patients develop chronic joint pain, and 10‐15 % experience persistent arthralgia for more than a year, with risk heightened in individuals over 45, women, and those with pre‐existing joint disease. Flare‐ups may be triggered by weather changes, physical strain, stress or intercurrent infections. Management includes NSAIDs (avoided until dengue is excluded), NSAID‐sparing DMARDs, physiotherapy, warm compresses, and anti‐inflammatory dietary measures, with specialist rheumatology referral advised if pain persists beyond 4‐6 weeks or is accompanied by swelling, redness, or prolonged morning stiffness.
